Acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma (alveoli and interstitium), usually infectious, presenting with fever, cough, and shortness of breath.
Pneumonia involving an entire lung lobe, most often caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and passing through four stages: congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, and resolution.
Patchy pneumonia centered on the bronchi and bronchioles with scattered foci of consolidation; common in the elderly and young children.
Pneumonia acquired outside the hospital or diagnosed within the first 48 hours of admission.
Pneumonia that develops 48 hours or more after hospital admission, often caused by antibiotic-resistant organisms.
Pneumonia caused by inhalation of gastric contents or oropharyngeal secretions into the lower airways.
Pneumonia caused by Pneumocystis jirovecii, seen mainly in people with HIV/AIDS and other forms of immunosuppression.
Chronic inflammation of the bronchi defined by a productive cough lasting at least 3 months per year for two consecutive years.
Short-lived inflammation of the bronchial mucosa, usually viral, causing cough that typically resolves within 2-3 weeks.
Chronic inflammatory airway disease with recurrent wheeze, breathlessness, and cough caused by reversible airflow obstruction and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
Severe, prolonged asthma attack unresponsive to standard bronchodilator therapy and threatening respiratory failure.
Progressive disease with persistent, not fully reversible airflow limitation, mainly caused by smoking and encompassing chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
Permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles with destruction of alveolar walls, reducing lung elasticity and causing dyspnea.
Irreversible dilation of the bronchi causing chronic cough with copious purulent sputum and recurrent infections.
Autosomal recessive disease caused by CFTR gene mutations that thicken exocrine secretions, affecting the lungs, pancreas, and sweat glands.
Localized, necrotic cavity of pus within the lung parenchyma, usually following aspiration or necrotizing infection.
Extensive, poorly demarcated necrosis of lung tissue caused by putrefactive organisms, with a severe clinical course.
Inflammation of the pleural layers causing sharp chest pain worsened by breathing, either dry or with fluid accumulation (effusion).
Abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, classified as transudate or exudate.
Collection of pus in the pleural space, usually as a complication of pneumonia or lung abscess.
Presence of air in the pleural space causing partial or complete lung collapse, presenting with sudden chest pain and dyspnea.
Life-threatening pneumothorax in which trapped air under pressure compresses the lung and shifts the mediastinum, requiring immediate decompression.
Accumulation of non-inflammatory transudative fluid in the pleural cavity, seen in heart failure, cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome.
Accumulation of blood in the pleural space, usually from chest trauma.
Collapse or incomplete expansion of part or all of a lung with loss of aerated volume.
Infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that mainly affects the lungs, causing prolonged cough, night sweats, and weight loss.
Multisystem disease of unknown cause marked by non-caseating granulomas, most often affecting the lungs and hilar lymph nodes.
Progressive scarring of the lung interstitium of unknown cause, leading to worsening dyspnea and dry cough.
Group of occupational lung diseases caused by inhalation of mineral dust with resulting fibrosis.
Pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged inhalation of crystalline silica dust, seen in miners and stone workers.
Pulmonary fibrosis caused by inhaling asbestos fibers, increasing the risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer.
Immune-mediated inflammation of the alveoli and interstitium in response to inhaled organic antigens, e.g., farmer's lung.
Obstruction of the pulmonary artery or its branches by a thrombus, usually from deep veins, causing sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
Necrosis of lung tissue resulting from occlusion of a pulmonary arterial branch.
Elevated mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mm Hg that increases right ventricular workload.
Enlargement and hypertrophy of the right ventricle caused by lung disease or pulmonary hypertension.
Accumulation of fluid in the alveoli and interstitium causing severe dyspnea and frothy pink sputum.
Acute respiratory failure from increased alveolar-capillary permeability, causing severe hypoxemia and bilateral lung infiltrates.
Inability of the lungs to adequately oxygenate the blood or eliminate carbon dioxide.
Recurrent collapse of the upper airway during sleep causing pauses in breathing, snoring, and daytime sleepiness.
Inflammation of the laryngeal mucosa that causes hoarseness.
Viral infection of the larynx and trachea in young children causing barking cough and inspiratory stridor.
Acute inflammation of the epiglottis that can rapidly obstruct the airway.
Inflammation of the paranasal sinus mucosa.
Inflammation of the nasal mucosa causing congestion and rhinorrhea.
IgE-mediated inflammation of the nasal mucosa triggered by allergens, causing sneezing and watery rhinorrhea.
Inflammation of the pharynx causing sore throat.
Inflammation of the palatine tonsils; group A streptococcal tonsillitis can lead to cardiac and renal complications.
Acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses, with high fever, myalgia, and cough.
Highly contagious infection caused by Bordetella pertussis, with paroxysmal coughing fits ending in a whooping inspiration.
Toxin-mediated infection by Corynebacterium diphtheriae causing a thick pharyngeal pseudomembrane and cardiac and neurologic complications.
Severe pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila, spread through contaminated water systems and air conditioning.
"Atypical" pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, with dry cough in school-age children and young adults.
Inflammation of the small bronchioles, usually due to respiratory syncytial virus in children under 2, causing wheeze and respiratory distress.
Chronic lung disease of premature infants resulting from prolonged oxygen therapy and mechanical ventilation.
Breathing difficulty in premature infants caused by surfactant deficiency and alveolar collapse.
Malignant tumor of the bronchi or lung tissue, divided into small cell and non-small cell types, with smoking as the main risk factor.
Malignant tumor of the pleura or other serous membranes, strongly associated with asbestos exposure.
Coughing up blood or blood-stained sputum from the respiratory tract.
Subjective sensation of breathlessness or difficulty breathing.
Bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to increased deoxygenated hemoglobin.
High-pitched, harsh breath sound produced by turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway.
Chronic elevation of arterial blood pressure, defined as systolic of 140 mm Hg or more and/or diastolic of 90 mm Hg or more on repeated measurements.
Primary arterial hypertension without an identifiable cause, accounting for most hypertension cases.
Hypertension caused by an identifiable underlying disorder such as renal or endocrine disease.
Severe acute rise in blood pressure, usually above 180/120 mm Hg, which may cause target-organ damage.
Sustained fall in blood pressure upon standing, causing dizziness or fainting.
Impaired blood supply to the myocardium due to narrowed coronary arteries, so that supply does not meet demand.
Retrosternal pressing or squeezing pain from myocardial ischemia, provoked by exertion and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
Angina occurring at rest or with minimal exertion with increasing frequency or severity, carrying a high risk of myocardial infarction.
Rest angina, often at night, caused by coronary artery spasm and accompanied by transient ST-segment elevation.
Necrosis of part of the heart muscle due to interrupted coronary blood flow, typically presenting with prolonged chest pain.
Myocardial infarction with ST-segment elevation on ECG caused by complete coronary occlusion, requiring urgent reperfusion.
Myocardial infarction with elevated troponin but no ST-segment elevation, typically from partial coronary occlusion.
Group of conditions, including unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, caused by acute coronary plaque rupture and thrombosis.
Replacement of necrotic myocardium with connective tissue scar after myocardial infarction.
Outward bulging of a scarred ventricular wall following myocardial infarction.
Inadequate tissue perfusion caused by severe failure of the heart's pumping function, a serious complication of myocardial infarction.
Inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet tissue needs, presenting with dyspnea, fatigue, and edema.
Sudden deterioration of cardiac pumping function that may present as cardiac asthma, pulmonary edema, or cardiogenic shock.
Attack of acute breathlessness, often nocturnal, caused by left ventricular failure.
Primary disease of the heart muscle not caused by valvular, coronary, or hypertensive disease.
Cardiomyopathy marked by enlarged cardiac chambers and reduced contractile function.
Often inherited cardiomyopathy with thickening of the ventricular wall, especially the septum, and a cause of sudden death in young athletes.
Cardiomyopathy in which stiff ventricular walls impair diastolic filling.
Inflammation of the myocardium, often following a viral infection.
Inflammation of the pericardium causing chest pain and a pericardial friction rub.
Compression of the heart by fluid or blood accumulating in the pericardial sac, impairing filling and requiring urgent drainage.
Microbial infection of the endocardium and heart valves with formation of vegetations.
Inflammatory disease following group A streptococcal infection that affects the heart, joints, and nervous system.
Chronic valvular damage, especially mitral stenosis, resulting from rheumatic fever.
Narrowing of the mitral valve orifice that obstructs left atrial emptying, causing left atrial enlargement and pulmonary congestion.
Backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium due to incomplete closure of the mitral valve.
Bulging of the mitral valve leaflets into the left atrium during systole.
Narrowing of the aortic valve, classically causing angina, syncope, and heart failure.
Diastolic backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle due to incompetence of the aortic valve.
Backflow of blood from the right ventricle to the right atrium due to tricuspid valve incompetence.
Structural abnormalities of the heart and great vessels present from birth.
Opening in the septum between the atria, producing a left-to-right shunt.
Opening in the septum between the ventricles, one of the most common congenital heart defects.
Failure of the fetal ductus arteriosus between the aorta and pulmonary artery to close after birth.
Cyanotic congenital defect with four features: pulmonary stenosis, ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Congenital narrowing of the aorta causing higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs.
Abnormality in the rate, regularity, or conduction of the heartbeat.
The most common sustained arrhythmia, with chaotic rapid atrial activity and irregularly irregular ventricular response, increasing stroke risk.
Rapid, regular atrial arrhythmia at about 300 beats per minute with a sawtooth pattern on ECG.
Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no effective pumping, a form of cardiac arrest requiring immediate defibrillation.
Rapid rhythm (over 100 beats per minute) originating in the ventricles.
Rapid, regular rhythm arising above the ventricles, in the atria or atrioventricular node.
Sinus-node rhythm with a heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
Sinus-node rhythm with a heart rate below 60 beats per minute.
Heartbeat occurring earlier than expected in the normal cycle.
Delay or interruption of impulse conduction from the atria to the ventricles, graded I to III.
Presence of an accessory atrioventricular pathway causing early ventricular activation (delta wave) and episodes of tachycardia.
Prolongation of the QT interval on ECG that predisposes to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.
Dysfunction of the sinus node causing alternating bradycardia and tachycardia.
Sudden cessation of effective cardiac contraction with loss of circulation and breathing.
Transient loss of consciousness due to temporary reduction of cerebral blood flow.
Disease in which cholesterol-rich plaques build up in arterial walls, narrowing the lumen.
Localized dilation of the aortic wall with a risk of rupture.
Tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to enter the vessel wall layers, causing sudden tearing chest or back pain.
Formation of a blood clot in the deep veins, usually of the leg, which may embolize to the lungs.
Inflammation of a vein with associated clot formation.
Dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins with incompetent valves.
Impaired venous return from the legs, producing edema, skin changes, and venous ulcers.
Narrowing of the leg arteries causing pain on walking (intermittent claudication) that eases with rest.
Episodic spasm of digital arteries causing finger pallor, cyanosis, and redness with cold or stress.
Group of diseases characterized by inflammation of blood vessel walls.
Chronic inflammation of the aorta and its major branches, more common in young women, causing diminished arm pulses.
Vasculitis of medium-sized arteries in children with prolonged fever, rash, mucosal redness, and risk of coronary aneurysms.
Abnormal levels of blood lipids such as cholesterol and triglycerides.
Elevated total or LDL cholesterol in the blood.
Cluster of abdominal obesity, hypertension, impaired glucose metabolism, and dyslipidemia that raises cardiovascular risk.
Life-threatening state of inadequate tissue perfusion leading to organ dysfunction.
Acute fall in blood pressure due to a sharp drop in vascular tone.
Fluid accumulation in the tissues, especially the legs, caused by heart failure.
Free fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity, seen in cirrhosis, heart failure, and other diseases.
